strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: evaluating frozen masked-image-modeling representations when standard linear probing poorly aggregates distributed patch information.

EP follows from a clean algebraic observation: key/query projections with a learned query can be collapsed into full-dimensional learned query vectors. The resulting module is simple, lightweight, and easy to implement.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering multiple MIM methods, backbone sizes, datasets, pretraining paradigms, and numerous attentive-pooling baselines. EP shows consistent accuracy gains and favorable parameter trade-offs.
Ablations of the key and value projections, query count, attention/output dimensions, intermediate layers, and limited-label settings provide useful evidence about the design.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with informative diagrams and attention visualizations.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is modest: EP is largely an algebraic reparameterization of learned-query attention into multiple linear attention scorers, closely related to existing MIL pooling and slot/query-based aggregation. The paper does not establish a deeper theoretical or algorithmic distinction.

The headline claim of an up-to-10x speed-up is not adequately supported. The evidence is probe-only GFLOPs, primarily against a full ViT block, rather than wall-clock throughput against the closest MHCA/AIM baseline. End-to-end cost including the frozen backbone and the claimed memory savings are not measured.

The accuracy-parameter comparison gives EP a substantially larger configuration search over query count and output dimension, while most competitors are shown at one configuration. The paper itself demonstrates that reducing the output dimension also benefits AIM; comparable sweeps and low-dimensional GAP/projection baselines are needed for a fair Pareto comparison.

Results lack repeated runs, error bars, or confidence intervals. Most benchmark values are available only through plots, and learning-rate selection appears to use the reported validation sets without a clearly separated model-selection protocol.

The interpretability conclusions are too strong. Attention mass inside bounding boxes and entropy are reported without box-area normalization, correlation coefficients, significance tests, or standard localization metrics. Replacing attention with a uniform map also makes the entropy relationship partly mechanical, while complementarity among queries is supported mainly by selected visual examples.

Reproducibility is incomplete: there is no code release, and important details such as initialization, weight decay, optimizer settings, schedules, checkpoint/layer choices, baseline-specific configurations, and selection of query count/output dimension are missing. Cross-paradigm rankings in Table 1 are additionally confounded by different architectures and pretraining datasets.

The central claim that EP is a better evaluation protocol for pretrained representations is not demonstrated. The advertised 10x 'speed-up over conventional multi-head attention' is not supported. The 10x number compares 0.12 GFLOPs for EP with a full ViT block at 1.44 GFLOPs, while the text says EP is comparable to vanilla MHCA. The accuracy comparisons lack repeated runs, error bars, or significance tests, although many advantages over strong attentive baselines are only a few tenths of a percentage point. EP receives an extensive sweep over query counts and output dimensions, whereas most competitors appear in one configuration, creating possible model-selection bias. Budget-matched comparisons with simple projected-GAP or similarly tuned baseline variants are insufficient.

The localization analysis does not support the strong claims about interpretability, robustness, avoidance of shortcut learning, or query specialization. No correlation coefficients, uncertainty estimates, diversity measures, background-shift tests, or controlled interventions are reported. In particular, replacing attention with a uniform distribution makes the entropy-versus-accuracy-drop relationship partly tautological: an already high-entropy map is necessarily changed less by that intervention.

Reproducibility is inadequate for the scale of the claims. There is no code release, random-seed information, complete optimizer and regularization configuration, checkpoint provenance, per-method hyperparameters, or precise split/model-selection protocol. The appendix supplies some training details, but not enough to reproduce or audit the extensive benchmark.

There are technical and presentation imprecisions. For example, the stated SimPool average q = X^T 1/N is dimensionally inconsistent with X in R^(Di x N); parameter accounting is unclear when the MHCA input vector u is described as learnable; and several broad statements such as fine-tuning being 'unsustainable' and EP providing robustness are stronger than the evidence.

Overall, the work is coherent and empirically promising, but its contribution is too incremental and its main efficiency, evaluation-validity, and interpretability claims are insufficiently supported for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

The central claim that EP is a better evaluation protocol is not demonstrated. Unlike a linear probe, EP is a supervised nonlinear, input-dependent aggregator that can learn substantial task-specific structure. Higher accuracy or altered model rankings therefore need not indicate better measurement of pretrained representation quality. Probe-capacity/selectivity controls or agreement with independent downstream evaluations are needed.

The parameter-efficiency comparisons are not fully controlled. EP alone receives extensive sweeps over output width and query count, while most competing poolers remain at their default width. Missing baselines include equally width-reduced AIM/other poolers and factorized low-rank CLS/GAP probes. The LoRA comparison is particularly affected because pure LoRA pays for a full-width classifier while EP and LoRA-plus-EP can shrink it, weakening the claimed strict Pareto dominance.

The efficiency evidence is incomplete: FLOPs exclude the 17.58-GFLOP backbone forward pass, so the reported greater-than-10-fold advantage concerns only the small head rather than end-to-end computation. There are no throughput, latency, training-memory, or wall-clock measurements despite an explicit claim of memory gains, and the experiments still run the frozen backbone every epoch.

No repeated trials, error bars, or significance tests are reported, even though many gains on strong modern encoders are only 0.4–1.1 points. Reproducibility is further limited by ambiguous method-specific tuning, initialization and implementation details, checkpoint provenance, and the absence of code; the described learning-rate search and model-selection protocol is also unclear.

The interpretability claims are overstated. EP attention is trained using ImageNet class labels, so Table 6 is weakly supervised rather than unsupervised localization, and comparison against frozen backbone attention does not control for supervision. Complementarity is strongly coupled to attention sharpness, qualitative examples may be selected, and no part annotations, correlation coefficients, uncertainty, or robustness experiments support the claimed semantic correspondence and robustness.

Several statements conflict with the reported evidence. The limitations claim exclusively frozen-backbone experiments and leave PEFT interaction and retrieval for future work, although both are already evaluated. Table 9 says EP at 10 epochs matches LP at 90 across models, but MAE ViT-B obtains 60.0 versus 67.7. Claims of consistent superiority likewise obscure cases where EP loses in raw accuracy or retrieval. These inconsistencies reduce confidence in the otherwise extensive study.

Implementation details use vague language such as “mostly” LARS and omit several optimizer, regularization, initialization, and competitor-specific tuning details; no code or configuration release is identified.

The interpretability conclusions are stronger than the analyses support. The localization–importance plots lack correlation coefficients or uncertainty and are confounded because replacing a high-entropy map with a uniform map inherently makes a smaller intervention. Complementarity comparisons do not control for attention temperature, sparsity, or task supervision, and the auxiliary complementarity loss does not improve EP's final accuracy. Calling localization “unsupervised” is also misleading because EP's attention was trained with ImageNet class labels, unlike the frozen-backbone attention baseline.

Several statements are inaccurate or overstated. EP is not always the most accurate method on downstream datasets, despite the abstract's unqualified outperformance claim. The convergence section says EP at 10 epochs matches or exceeds 90-epoch LP across all 12 models, but MAE ViT-B obtains 60.0% versus 67.7%. The limitations section also says interaction with PEFT and tasks beyond classification remain unexplored despite the paper already presenting LoRA+EP, localization, and retrieval experiments. These inconsistencies reduce confidence in the presentation.

The empirical breadth is a major strength. Results cover numerous attentive-pooling baselines, seven classification datasets, multiple model sizes, and pretraining paradigms including MIM, joint-embedding, hybrid, vision-language, diffusion, and autoregressive models.

weaknesses: The methodological novelty is modest. EP is principally the algebraic collapse of a learned key projection and query into a directly learned effective query, closely related to existing learned-query pooling, AbMILP, and simplified slot-attention constructions. The central parameter-efficiency comparison lacks decisive parameter-matched controls, especially low-rank/factorized linear probing and CLS/GAP plus a learnable value bottleneck at each tested output dimension. The empirical scope is unusually broad, covering numerous backbones and pre-training paradigms, seven classification datasets, many attentive-pooling baselines, parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods, and both parameter and FLOP trade-offs.

EP produces consistent and sometimes large improvements over linear probing, especially for masked, autoregressive, and diffusion pre-training whose information is distributed across patch tokens. The LoRA+EP results also provide useful evidence that attentive pooling and backbone adaptation can be complementary.

The paper includes substantial ablation and diagnostic work on query count, key/value projections, output dimension, convergence, low-shot learning, intermediate layers, localization, retrieval, and attention diversity. Presentation and figures are generally clear.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited. EP is principally an algebraic reparameterization of fixed-query cross-attention plus a straightforward multi-query extension of learned attention pooling, a broadly established design pattern. The positioning does not adequately distinguish it from prior multi-seed or learned-query set-pooling mechanisms, making the claim of a novel attention mechanism too strong.

The central Pareto comparison is not fully controlled. EP is extensively swept over query count and output dimension, whereas most competing methods use full output dimension and largely fixed designs. Important matched-budget baselines—such as GAP or CLS pooling followed by a learned low-dimensional projection, a factorized low-rank linear probe, and similarly tuned output bottlenecks for every attentive baseline—are missing from the main comparison. Thus, some low-parameter advantage may come from a generally applicable bottleneck rather than EP specifically.

Optimization fairness and statistical reliability are insufficiently established. ImageNet and Places365 use one fixed learning rate despite very different heads, while repurposed transformer-style baselines may require different optimizers or schedules. No repeated runs, error bars, or significance analyses are reported, which matters for the many claimed gains of only 0.4–0.8 percentage points.

The paper does not establish that EP is a better representation-evaluation protocol rather than merely a more expressive supervised head. It is nonlinear and task-trained, changes model rankings, and receives additional capacity relative to linear probing, but the authors do not systematically show that its rankings better predict full fine-tuning or broad downstream transfer.

Several secondary claims exceed the evidence. Attention diversity does not by itself imply semantic complementarity or interpretability, the localization–accuracy plots lack correlation coefficients and uncertainty, and no robustness benchmark supports the claimed robustness gains. Calling the localization experiment “unsupervised” is also misleading because EP was trained using ImageNet class labels; the appropriate framing is weakly supervised localization.

Reproducibility is incomplete: there is no code link, seed information, variance reporting, or sufficient detail for several optimizer, k-NN, retrieval, and initialization choices. There is also a concrete textual contradiction: the appendix says EP after 10 epochs matches or exceeds 90-epoch LP across all 12 models, but MAE ViT-B scores 60.0 versus 67.7. Compute claims additionally emphasize head-only FLOPs while excluding the frozen-backbone forward pass that dominates practical training cost.
